citations.quote: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Phi(x)=P(Z\le x)$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Then $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Phi(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\Phi(x)=1$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume AC. For $d\ge1$, let $\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^d$,
let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be Borel, and let
$A+rB_2^d=\{a+ru:a\in A,\ |u|\le1\}$. Then for every $r\ge0$,
$$\gamma_{d,*}(A+rB_2^d)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_d(A))+r\right),$$
where $\gamma_{d,*}(S)=\sup\{\gamma_d(K):K\subseteq S,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ is Gaussian inner measure, and $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Assume AC. Under the hypotheses and notation of
[[def-banach-gaussian-covariance-operator-and-rkhs]], each $C\ell$ exists as a
Bochner integral; $Q$ is a finite positive-semidefinite bilinear form;
$N=\{\ell:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$ is its nullspace; and the induced map from the
completion of $B^*/N$ to $B$ is continuous and injective. Thus the definition
identifies a Hilbert space of shifts in $B$.

Assume AC. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subset B$ be its covariance RKHS. The closed Hilbert
unit ball
$$H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$$
is compact in the Banach norm.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Assume HB and let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. For each $x\ne0$ there is $f\in X^*$ with $\|f\|=1$ and $f(x)=\|x\|$, a positive real number also in the complex case. Hence $X^*$ separates distinct points, and
$$\|x\|=\max_{f\in X^*,\ \|f\|\le1}|f(x)|\qquad(x\in X).$$
The formula includes $x=0$ and the zero space. Moreover, if $H\subseteq X^*$ has norm-dense scalar-linear span and $h(x)=0$ for all $h\in H$, then $x=0$.

derivations.claim: First let $F=T^{-1}(M)$ be a closed finite-coordinate cylinder, with $T=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k):B\to\mathbb R^k$ continuous and $M$ closed. Let $Q=\operatorname{span}\{[\ell_i]:1\le i\le k\}\subset H$, choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, and choose representatives $\varphi_j\in B^*$ for $e_j$. Set $G=\sum_{j=1}^m\varphi_j(W)e_j$ and $S=T\circ i|_Q$. The vector of coefficients is standard Gaussian on $Q$ because its covariance matrix is the identity. For each $i$, $[\ell_i]=\sum_j\langle[\ell_i],e_j\rangle_H e_j$; by the covariance quotient and [F2], the residual $\ell_i(W)-\ell_i(iG)$ has variance $\|[\ell_i]-\sum_j\langle[\ell_i],e_j\rangle_H e_j\|_H^2=0$. Hence $T(W)=S(G)$ almost surely. The map $S$ is injective: if $S(q)=0$, then $\langle q,[\ell_i]\rangle_H=0$ for every $i$, and these classes span $Q$, so $q=0$.

Now let $A\subseteq B$ be Borel with $0<\mu(A)<1$, and fix $ eta<\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))$. By [F4] choose compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(K)>\Phi( eta)$. For each $x
otin K$ and $y\in K$, [F7] gives $\ell_y\in B^*$ with $\ell_y(x)
e\ell_y(y)$. The open sets $U_y=\{z:|\ell_y(z)-\ell_y(y)|<|\ell_y(x)-\ell_y(y)|/3\}$ cover $K$; compactness gives a finite subcover $U_{y_1},\ldots,U_{y_q}$. For every $z\in K$, some $i$ has $z\in U_{y_i}$, which forces $\ell_{y_i}(z)
e\ell_{y_i}(x)$. Thus the finite coordinate map $T_x=(\ell_{y_1},\ldots,\ell_{y_q})$ satisfies $T_x(x)
otin T_x(K)$. The cylinder $F_x=T_x^{-1}(T_x(K))$ is closed, contains $K$, and excludes $x$, since $T_x(K)$ is compact. The open complements $B\setminus F_x$ cover $B\setminus K$. By [F5] this cover has a countable subcover: for every basis element meeting $B\setminus K$ and contained in a cover member, countable choice selects one such member; every point is covered by one selected member. If the subcover is finite, repeat one member to index it by $j\ge1$.

If $m=0$, then $T(W)=0$ almost surely, so $\mu(F)$ is zero or one; the endpoint convention, $0\in H_1$, and inner regularity [F4] give the claimed inequality. If $m>0$, define $E=S^{-1}(M)\subset Q$. It is closed and $\mu(F)=\gamma_Q(E)$. For $r\ge0$, $E_r=E+r(Q\cap H_1)$ is closed because its second summand is compact. Thus [F4] identifies its inner and ordinary Gaussian measures, and [F1] gives $\gamma_Q(E_r)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\gamma_Q(E))+r)$. Let $C_r=T^{-1}(S(E_r))$, a closed finite-coordinate cylinder because $S$ is a linear isomorphism from finite-dimensional $Q$ onto the closed subspace $S(Q)$; injectivity of $S$ and $T(W)=S(G)$ give $\mu(C_r)=\gamma_Q(E_r)$. If $y\in C_r$, write $T(y)=S(u+v)$ with $u\in E$ and $v\in r(Q\cap H_1)$. Then $T(y-i(v))=S(u)\in M$, so $y-i(v)\in F$ and $y\in F+rH_1$. Hence $C_r\subseteq F+rH_1$, and inner regularity [F4] gives $\mu_*(F+rH_1)\ge\mu(C_r)\ge\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(\mu(F))+r)$.

Let $G_n=\bigcap_{j\le n}F_{x_j}$ for the countable subcover in step 1.2. Each $G_n$ is a closed finite-coordinate cylinder because it is a finite intersection of such cylinders; the sequence decreases, $\bigcap_nG_n=K$, and $\mu(G_n)\ge\mu(K)>\Phi(\beta)$. Applying step 2.1 yields $\mu_*(G_n+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. The set $G_n+rH_1$ is closed: if $a_j+h_j$ converges with $a_j\in G_n$ and $h_j\in rH_1$, compactness [F3] gives a convergent subsequence of $h_j$, after which closedness of $G_n$ gives a limit representation. Thus [F4] gives equality of its inner and ordinary measures.

The closed sets $G_n+rH_1$ decrease and their intersection is $K+rH_1$. Indeed, if $x=a_n+h_n$ with $a_n\in G_n$ and $h_n\in rH_1$ for every $n$, compactness [F3] gives a subsequence $h_{n_j}\to h\in rH_1$; then $a_{n_j}\to x-h$, and for each fixed $N$ the tail belongs to the closed set $G_N$, so $x-h\in K$. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Continuity from above [F6] gives $\mu(K+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. Since $K\subseteq A$, $\mu_*(A+rH_1)\ge\Phi(\beta+r)$. Letting $\beta\uparrow\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))$ proves the interior-probability case. If $\mu(A)=0$ the right side is zero; if $\mu(A)=1$, inner regularity [F4] and $0\in H_1$ give $\mu_*(A+rH_1)=1$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$. For
$\varepsilon>0$, write
$\varepsilon B^\circ=\{x\in B:\|x\|_B<\varepsilon\}$ and define the
**concentration function**
$$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon) =\inf_{\substack{h\in H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon}} \left\{\|h\|_H^2-\log\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)\right\}.$$
The feasible set is nonempty because $w_0$ lies in the Banach-norm closure of
$H$. Also $\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)>0$ because $0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$;
thus the logarithm is finite. The value is finite and nonnegative. The support assertion used here is
[[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]].

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$ and covariance RKHS $H\subseteq B$. For
$h\in H$, let $z_h$ be the $L^2(\mu)$-limit of the coordinate functions
$\ell(x)$ representing a sequence of classes $[\ell]\to i^{-1}h$ in the
completion $H$. The limit has a $\mu$-measurable version and does not depend
on the approximating sequence. If $\mu_h$ denotes the law of $W+h$, then
$$\frac{d\mu_h}{d\mu}(x) =\exp\!\left(z_h(x)-\frac12\|h\|_H^2\right).$$
In particular, $\mu_h$ and $\mu$ are equivalent. If $h=C\ell$ for
$\ell\in B^*$, then $z_h(x)=\ell(x)$ $\mu$-almost surely and
$\|h\|_H^2=E[\ell(W)^2]$; these formulas are independent of the choice of
representative $\ell$.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$ and unit ball $H_1$. For every Borel set
$A\subseteq B$ and $r\ge0$,
$$\mu_*(A+rH_1)\ge \Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(\mu(A))+r\right),$$
where $\mu_*(S)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subseteq S,\ K\text{ compact}\}$ is the inner
measure and $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$. When
$A+rH_1$ is Borel, its inner measure equals its ordinary $\mu$-measure.

Assume AC. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subset B$ be its covariance RKHS. The closed Hilbert
unit ball
$$H_1=\{h\in H:\|h\|_H\le1\}$$
is compact in the Banach norm.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Assume HB and countable choice. Let $B$ be a real separable Banach space. There is a sequence
$(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ with $\|\ell_j\|=1$ such that
$$\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|\qquad(x\in B).$$
If $B=\{0\}$, the conclusion is interpreted using the zero functional and the
supremum is $0$.

Let $B$ be a separable Banach space, and let $(\ell_j)_{j\ge1}\subseteq B^*$ satisfy the norming identity $\|x\|=\sup_{j\ge1}|\ell_j(x)|$ for every $x\in B$. If Borel probabilities $\mu,\nu$ on $B$ have equal finite-dimensional pushforwards under every finite subfamily of $(\ell_j)$, then $\mu=\nu$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random
element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$ and covariance RKHS $H\subseteq B$. For
$h\in H$, let $z_h$ be the $L^2(\mu)$-limit of the coordinate functions
$\ell(x)$ representing a sequence of classes $[\ell]\to i^{-1}h$ in the
completion $H$. The limit has a $\mu$-measurable version and does not depend
on the approximating sequence. If $\mu_h$ denotes the law of $W+h$, then
$$\frac{d\mu_h}{d\mu}(x) =\exp\!\left(z_h(x)-\frac12\|h\|_H^2\right).$$
In particular, $\mu_h$ and $\mu$ are equivalent. If $h=C\ell$ for
$\ell\in B^*$, then $z_h(x)=\ell(x)$ $\mu$-almost surely and

derivations.claim: The hypothesis [F1] implies $p\ge e^{-t}>0$, because every candidate $h$ has $\|h\|_H^2\ge0$. Fix $h\in H$. Take a countable norming family for $B$ and append the scalar coordinate $z_h$; this is a countable norming family for $B\times\mathbb R$ with the maximum product norm. By [F7], each finite coordinate vector is centered Gaussian and hence invariant under negation, so countable law determination makes the joint law symmetric under $(x,z)\mapsto(-x,-z)$. Thus, since $\varepsilon B^\circ$ is symmetric, $\int_{\varepsilon B^\circ}e^{-z_h(x)}\,d\mu(x) =\int_{\varepsilon B^\circ}\cosh(z_h(x))\,d\mu(x) \ge p.$ The Cameron–Martin identity [F2] for $-h$ now gives $\mu(h+\varepsilon B^\circ)\ge e^{-\|h\|_H^2/2}p$.

For each $\delta>0$, choose $h\in H$ with $\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon$ and $\|h\|_H^2-\log p<\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)+\delta\le t+\delta$. Since $\|h\|_H^2/2-\log p\le\|h\|_H^2-\log p<t+\delta$, and $h+\varepsilon B^\circ\subset w_0+2\varepsilon B^\circ$, step 1.1 gives $\mu\{\|W-w_0\|_B<2\varepsilon\}\ge e^{-t-\delta}$. Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ proves the small-ball lower bound.

Let $b=\Phi^{-1}(e^{-Ct})<0$ and $M=-2b>0$, and set $B_n=\varepsilon B^\circ+MH_1$. This is open, hence measurable. Since $p\ge e^{-t}$ and $C>1$, monotonicity of $\Phi^{-1}$ gives $\Phi^{-1}(p)>b$. By [F3], $\mu(B_n)\ge \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(p)+M) >\Phi(-b)=1-e^{-Ct}.$ The set $B_n$ is open and therefore Borel, so [F6] identifies its inner measure with $\mu(B_n)$. Thus $\mu(B\setminus B_n)\le e^{-Ct}$.

Choose a maximal finite set $\{h_1,\ldots,h_N\}\subset MH_1$ with pairwise distances greater than $2\varepsilon$; such a set exists and covers $MH_1$ by closed $2\varepsilon$-balls because $MH_1$ is compact by [F4]. The open balls $h_i+\varepsilon B^\circ$ are disjoint. Step 1.1 and $\|h_i\|_H\le M$ imply each has $\mu$-measure at least $e^{-M^2/2}p$. Hence $N e^{-M^2/2}p\le1$ and $\log N\le M^2/2-\log p\le M^2/2+t$. Every point of $B_n$ lies within $3\varepsilon$ of one of the $h_i$, so $N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le N$.

Completing the square in the standard normal density [F5] gives $E e^{-\lambda Z}=e^{\lambda^2/2}$. For $x\ge0$, on $\{Z\le-x\}$ one has $e^{-xZ}\ge e^{x^2}$, so $\Phi(-x)=P(Z\le-x)\le e^{-x^2}E e^{-xZ}=e^{-x^2/2}$. With $x=\sqrt{2Ct}$ this gives $\Phi(-\sqrt{2Ct})\le e^{-Ct}=\Phi(b)$, hence $-\sqrt{2Ct}\le b<0$ and $b^2\le2Ct$. Consequently $\log N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le2b^2+t\le4Ct+t\le5Ct\le6Ct$, using $C>1$. Step 2.2 supplies the complement bound and step 2.1 the small-ball bound. No posterior statement follows from these three prior inequalities alone.

derivations.claim: On the event $\{\|W\|_B<\epsilon\}$, continuity and linearity give $|\ell(W)|\le\|\ell\|_{B^*}\|W\|_B<\|\ell\|_{B^*}\epsilon$. The interval $(-\|\ell\|\epsilon,\|\ell\|\epsilon)$ has length $2\|\ell\|\epsilon$, so its scalar Gaussian probability is at most its length times the density bound in [F1]. Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, and let $H\subseteq B$ be its covariance RKHS. Define
$\operatorname{supp}\mu$ to be the set of $x\in B$ for which every open
neighborhood has positive $\mu$-measure. Then
$$\operatorname{supp}\mu=\overline H^{\,B}.$$

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$. For
$\varepsilon>0$, write
$\varepsilon B^\circ=\{x\in B:\|x\|_B<\varepsilon\}$ and define the
**concentration function**
$$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon) =\inf_{\substack{h\in H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\varepsilon}} \left\{\|h\|_H^2-\log\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)\right\}.$$
The feasible set is nonempty because $w_0$ lies in the Banach-norm closure of
$H$. Also $\mu(\varepsilon B^\circ)>0$ because $0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$;
thus the logarithm is finite. The value is finite and nonnegative. The support assertion used here is
[[thm-support-of-banach-gaussian-is-closure-of-rkhs]].

Assume AC and countable choice. Let $\mu$ be a centered tight Borel Gaussian
law on a real separable Banach
space $B$, with covariance RKHS $H$, and let $w_0\in\overline H^{\,B}$.
Suppose $n\ge1$, $\varepsilon>0$, $C>1$,
$e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2}<1/2$, and
$\phi_{w_0}(\varepsilon)\le n\varepsilon^2$, where $\phi_{w_0}$ is the
concentration function. Then there is a measurable set $B_n\subseteq B$
such that
$$\log N(3\varepsilon,B_n,\|\cdot\|_B)\le6Cn\varepsilon^2,\qquad \mu(B\setminus B_n)\le e^{-Cn\varepsilon^2},$$
and
$$\mu\{\|W-w_0\|_B<2\varepsilon\}\ge e^{-n\varepsilon^2}.$$
These are prior-mass and sieve bounds only; they assert no posterior
contraction without separate statistical-distance and Kullback–Leibler
comparisons.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let $B$ be a real
separable Banach space with its norm Borel sigma-algebra. A map
$W:\Omega\to B$ is a **centered Borel Gaussian random element** if it is
Borel-measurable and, for every $\ell\in B^*$, the real random variable
$\ell(W)$ has a centered (possibly zero-variance) normal law. Its law is the
Borel probability $\mu=P\circ W^{-1}$. When the word *tight* is used, it means
that for every $\delta>0$ there is a norm-compact $K\subseteq B$ with
$\mu(K)>1-\delta$.

This definition concerns a random element in $B$. A Gaussian process on an
arbitrary index set with only a cylinder-space law does not satisfy it unless
a Borel $B$-valued realization is separately constructed.

Assume AC. Let $W$ be a centered Borel Gaussian random element in a real separable
Banach space $B$, with law $\mu$. For $\ell\in B^*$ define
$$C\ell=E[\ell(W)W]\in B,\qquad Q(\ell,m)=E[\ell(W)m(W)]\quad(\ell,m\in B^*).$$
The **Cameron–Martin reproducing-kernel Hilbert space** $H$ is the completion
of $B^*/N$ in the inner product induced by $Q$, where
$N=\{\ell\in B^*:Q(\ell,\ell)=0\}$. The canonical map sends the class of
$\ell$ to $C\ell$ and extends continuously to an injective map $i:H\to B$;
we identify $H$ with its image in $B$ and use the completed Hilbert norm
$\|\cdot\|_H$. The preceding construction is well-defined by
[[thm-banach-gaussian-covariance-rkhs-is-well-defined]].

The term *RKHS* here denotes this covariance-induced Hilbert space of shifts
inside $B$; it is not the space of all continuous functions on an arbitrary
index set.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space with a fixed sigma-finite measure. A probability density is a finite-valued nonnegative measurable $p$ with $\int p\,d\mu=1$, and its induced law is $P_p=p\,d\mu$ as in [[def-measure-with-density]]. Let $p_0$ be a probability density and write $P_0:=p_0\,d\mu$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a family of such densities, write $P_p:=p\,d\mu$ for $p\in\mathcal F$, and let $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F$ be nonempty. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID under each law used below. The selected metric $d$ is one of:

- the root-L2 Hellinger distance $h$ of [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]];
- the full density distance $d_1(p,q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$;
- the density distance $d_2(p,q):=(\int|p-q|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}$, provided a fixed $B>0$ bounds $p_0$ and every $p\in\mathcal F$ by $B$ almost everywhere.

For $r>0$, let $D(r,\mathcal F_n,d)$ be the supremum of the cardinalities of finite subsets of $\mathcal F_n$ whose distinct points have $d$-distance greater than $r$. Suppose $\epsilon_n>0$, $\epsilon_n\to0$, $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, and
$$\log D(\epsilon_n,\mathcal F_n,d)\le n\epsilon_n^2.$$
Then for every fixed $M\ge128$ and all sufficiently large $n$, there is a measurable test $\phi_n:\mathsf X^n\to\{0,1\}$ such that, for some $c_d>0$ depending only on the selected metric (and on $B$ in the $d_2$ case),
$$P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le2e^{-(c_dM^2-1)n\epsilon_n^2},$$
and $P_p^n(\phi_n=0)\le e^{-c_dM^2n\epsilon_n^2}$ for every $p\in\mathcal F_n$ with $d(p,p_0)>M\epsilon_n$.

The entropy metric is the same metric used in the separation and test-error conclusion. The $d_1$ convention is the full integral $\int|p-q|\,d\mu$, which equals twice the library event-supremum total variation distance.

Let $G$ be a probability measure on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, let $\Psi:\mathbb R\to(0,1)$ be differentiable, and suppose
$$L:=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}|\Psi'(u)|<\infty,\qquad R:=\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\left|\frac{\Psi'(u)}{\Psi(u)(1-\Psi(u))}\right|<\infty.$$
For measurable real functions $w,w_0$, define Bernoulli densities relative to $G\otimes\#$, where $\#$ is counting measure on $\{0,1\}$, by
$$q_w(x,y)=\Psi(w(x))^y(1-\Psi(w(x)))^{1-y},\qquad q_{w_0}(x,y)=\Psi(w_0(x))^y(1-\Psi(w_0(x)))^{1-y}.$$
If $w-w_0\in L^2(G)$, then, with $d_2(q_w,q_{w_0})^2=\int|q_w-q_{w_0}|^2\,d(G\otimes\#)$,
$$d_2(q_w,q_{w_0})^2\le2L^2\|w-w_0\|_{L^2(G)}^2,$$

Let $B$ be a real Banach space and let $W$ be a Borel measurable $B$-valued random element with tight law $\mu$. Tight means that for every $\eta>0$ some compact $K\subset B$ satisfies $\mu(K)>1-\eta$. Assume $W$ is centered Gaussian, meaning that every continuous real linear functional $\ell:B\to\mathbb R$ makes $\ell(W)$ a centered scalar normal random variable. Then there is a separable closed linear subspace $E\subset B$ with $\mu(E)=1$. The law of $W$ viewed as an $E$-valued random element is tight and centered Gaussian, and its support in $E$ is exactly the support of $\mu$ in $B$, viewed as a subset of $B$. $x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The separable-support reduction [F5] leaves the inherited norm, law and support point unchanged. For the first two branches use the rate $r_n=\epsilon_n$; for the universal fixed-design branch use $r_n=\rho_n$. The concentration function is nonincreasing in its radius, because its feasible RKHS approximation set grows and centered small-ball probabilities increase. Thus $\phi_{w_0}(r_n)\le\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2\le nr_n^2$. Both choices satisfy $r_n\to0$ and $nr_n^2\to\infty$. By [F8], the support point lies in the RKHS closure.

In log-Gaussian density estimation, evaluation measurability and Tonelli [F6] make $w\mapsto Z_w$ measurable. On its full-prior positive-finite set, $(w,x)\mapsto e^{w(x)}/Z_w$ is a jointly measurable density family. The $2r_n$ supremum ball has directional KL at most $2e^{4r_n}r_n^2$ and log-square at most $16r_n^2$ by [F3]. Choose a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its prior mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] at radius $kr_n$ gives a denominator at least $e^{-A nr_n^2}$ for fixed $A=1+2k^2$ except with probability tending to zero.

In binary regression, [F3] places the $2r_n$ prior ball in a directional KL/log-square set of radius $k^2r_n^2$ for a fixed sufficiently large $k$. Its mass is at least $e^{-nr_n^2}$ by [F10], so [F1] gives the same type of denominator bound. The joint Bernoulli densities relative to $G\otimes\#$ are bounded by one, as required for the density-$L^2$ tests in [F2].

Independence and [A2], together with [F10], give joint local prior mass at least $cr_ne^{-nr_n^2}$. Since $r_n\ge\sqrt{\log n/n}$, eventually $\log(1/r_n)\le\tfrac12\log n\le\tfrac12nr_n^2$; hence this mass is at least $e^{-C_0nr_n^2}$ for fixed $C_0$. The independent-observation denominator lemma in [F4] applies.

The same theorem supplies the local prior mass used in steps 1.2–1.4.

In the density branch intersect $B_n$ with the measurable positive-finite-normalizer set, changing its prior tail by zero. From a radius-$3r_n$ cover, select a valid center for every cover ball meeting that intersection; finite selection doubles the radius to $6r_n$ without increasing the number. The pairwise norm comparison [F3] sends this to a Hellinger cover of radius at most $7r_n$ for large $n$. Thus any $14r_n$-separated set has size at most $e^{6Cnr_n^2}$. In fixed-design regression take the product sieve $B_n\times[a,b]$. Its prior tail is at most $e^{-Cnr_n^2}$, and its function component has the radius-$3r_n$ cover from step 2.1. If the Gaussian law is not $\delta_0$, [F13] supplies a continuous linear functional with nonzero Gaussian variance. In each proved branch the posterior tail is a random variable $T_n\in[0,1]$ converging to zero in probability. For $\eta>0$, $ET_n\le\eta+P(T_n>\eta)$; first take the limit superior and then $\eta\downarrow0$. Thus all asserted expectation limits follow. The universal fixed-design rate requires no upper bound on the scale density; the sharper degenerate alternative uses only the explicitly local upper bound.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Let $\epsilon_n>0$ satisfy $\epsilon_n\to0$ and $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. For the centered tight Gaussian prior in each branch, let $\mu$ be its law and let $B$ be a separable closed Banach carrier with the norm inherited from that branch's stated function space, as supplied by [[lem-tight-borel-gaussian-law-has-separable-support]]. Write $\mathbb H$ for the covariance RKHS of $\mu$ on $B$, and define
$$\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon)=\inf_{\substack{h\in\mathbb H\\\|h-w_0\|_B<\epsilon}}\left\{\|h\|_{\mathbb H}^2-\log\mu(\epsilon B^\circ)\right\},\qquad \epsilon B^\circ=\{u\in B:\|u\|_B<\epsilon\}.$$
Suppose $\phi_{w_0}(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2$.

In each branch, parameter-to-data densities are jointly measurable and the posterior $\Pi_n$ is the data-indexed normalization of the prior times the likelihood on fibers with finite positive evidence.

1. **Log-Gaussian density estimation.** On a measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ with sigma-finite measure $\nu$, let $W$ be a tight centered Borel Gaussian random element in $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$, and let $w_0$ belong to its support. Assume path evaluation $(w,x)\mapsto w(x)$ is jointly measurable, $Z_w=\int e^w\,d\nu\in(0,\infty)$ for prior-almost every $w$ and for $w_0$, and set $p_w=e^w/Z_w$, $p_0=p_{w_0}$. For IID data $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_0$, sufficiently large fixed $M$ gives
$$E_0\Pi_n\{w:h(P_w,P_0)>M\epsilon_n\mid X^n\}\longrightarrow0.$$
When $0<\nu(\mathsf X)<\infty$, bounded paths imply the required normalizers are finite and positive.

2. **Binary regression.** Let $(X_i,Y_i)$ be IID, with $X_i\sim G$, $Y_i\in\{0,1\}$ and $P_0(Y=1\mid X=x)=f_0(x)=\Psi(w_0(x))\in(0,1)$. Assume $\Psi:\mathbb R\to(0,1)$ is differentiable, $\sup|\Psi'|<\infty$, and $\sup|\Psi'/[\Psi(1-\Psi)]|<\infty$. Suppose the prior is either a tight centered Gaussian law in $L^2(G)$ with a jointly measurable evaluation version representing its $L^2(G)$ element almost everywhere, or a tight centered Gaussian law in $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$ with jointly measurable evaluation and bounded $w_0$; in either case $w_0$ belongs to the prior support. Then for sufficiently large fixed $M$,
$$E_0\Pi_n\{\|\Psi(w)-f_0\|_{L^2(G)}>M\epsilon_n\mid (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n\}\longrightarrow0.$$

3. **Fixed-design Gaussian regression.** For deterministic $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, assume independent $Y_i\sim N(w_0(x_i),\sigma_0^2)$, a centered tight Borel Gaussian prior $W$ in $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$ with $w_0$ in support, and an independent prior on the standard deviation $\sigma$ supported on a fixed $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $\sigma_0$, with Lebesgue density bounded below by a positive constant. Put $\rho_n=\max\{\epsilon_n,\sqrt{\log n/n}\}$ for $n\ge2$. Then for sufficiently large fixed $M$,
$$E_0\Pi_n\{\|w-w_0\|_n+|\sigma-\sigma_0|>M\rho_n\mid Y_{1:n}\}\longrightarrow0.$$
The sharper conclusion with $\epsilon_n$ in place of $\rho_n$ holds if the Gaussian law is not the point mass at zero. It also holds when $W=0$ almost surely and the scale-prior density is bounded above on a neighborhood of $\sigma_0$; this extra upper bound is needed only for that sharper degenerate-prior alternative, not for the universal $\rho_n$ conclusion. In the nondegenerate case $\rho_n=O(\epsilon_n)$, so the two formulations differ only by the fixed constant $M$. Here $\|w-w_0\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(w(x_i)-w_0(x_i))^2$.

The concentration-function hypothesis is interpreted on a separable Banach space carrying the prior. For a tight Gaussian law initially given in nonseparable $\ell^\infty(\mathsf X)$, the separable-support reduction is [[lem-tight-borel-gaussian-law-has-separable-support]]; the norm and prior law are restricted to that support space.

derivations.claim: Every prior path is constant, so $Z_W=\int_0^1 e^Zdx=e^Z$ and $p_W(x)=1=p_0(x)$. Thus the posterior distribution of the density itself is the point mass at $p_0$ for every data vector; its posterior mass outside every positive Hellinger ball is exactly zero.

The RKHS approximation term at $w_0=0$ is zero because the zero vector belongs to every Hilbert space. For $0<\epsilon\le1$, [F1] gives $\Pr(\|W\|_\infty<\epsilon)=\Pr(|Z|<\epsilon)\ge2\varphi(1)\epsilon$, hence $\phi_0(\epsilon)\le-\log(2\varphi(1)\epsilon)$. For $\epsilon_n=\sqrt{\log n/n}$, $n\epsilon_n^2=\log n$ and $-\log\epsilon_n\le\frac12\log n$ for large n, so $\phi_0(\epsilon_n)\le n\epsilon_n^2$ eventually.

The density family is jointly measurable and all normalizers are positive and finite. Step 1.2 verifies the concentration premise; applying the log-Gaussian branch of [F2] gives the stated rate, while step 1.1 gives the stronger exact posterior conclusion.

$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by

Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Assume AC. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be independent $N(0,1)$ variables, let $c_1,\ldots,c_n,\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_n\in\mathbb R$, and let $0<\sigma\le b$. Put $\|c\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i c_i^2$ and $\|\delta\|_n^2=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_i^2$. For $t>0$,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i c_i\sigma Z_i\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{2\sigma^2\|c\|_n^2}\right),$$
with zero probability when $\|c\|_n=0$. If $\|\delta\|_n\le1$ and $0<t\le b^2+2$, then
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|n^{-1}\sum_i(\delta_i+\sigma Z_i)^2-(\sigma^2+\|\delta\|_n^2)\right|\ge t\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{nt^2}{4V_b}\right),\qquad V_b=2b^4+4b^2.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
